`memmove` is a standard C library function that is used to copy a block of memory from one location to another. The `memmove` function is similar to the `memcpy` function, but it can handle overlapping source and destination regions.

The function is declared in the `string.h` header file and has the following prototype:
```c
void *memmove(void *dest, const void *src, size_t n);
```
The `memmove` function takes three arguments:

* `dest` is a pointer to the destination array where the data will be copied.
* `src` is a pointer to the source array from where the data will be copied.
* `n` is the number of bytes to be copied.

The `memmove` function copies the `n` bytes of memory from the source array to the destination array. If the source and destination arrays overlap, the function ensures that the data is correctly copied by using a temporary buffer to hold the data during the copy operation.

The function returns a pointer to the destination array.

1. Open your user settings by clicking on "Preferences: Open User Settings" in the Command Palette (Cmd/Ctrl + Shift + P) or by opening the Settings editor and clicking on the "Open Settings (JSON)" button in the top right corner.
2. In the settings editor, add the following line to associate the ".Dockerfile" extension with the Dockerfile language mode:
```json
"files.associations": {
    "*.Dockerfile": "dockerfile"
}
```
This tells VS Code to treat any file with the extension ".Dockerfile" as a Dockerfile and enable syntax highlighting and other features for the Dockerfile language.

You can replace ".Dockerfile" with any other file extension you want to use for your Dockerfiles.

Once you've added this line to your settings, VS Code will recognize any files with the specified extension as Dockerfiles and provide the appropriate features.

The authors of this study examine the role of working memory in attentional guidance. They propose that attentional templates integrate target features (such as a purple chair) to guide attention in an object-based fashion, or that they are established for each target feature individually. The results of their experiment suggest that attentional guidance by irrelevant features depends on their successful encoding into working memory, and that effects of irrelevant features are easier to observe when they are presented as part of an object rather than separately. However, guidance by separate features is possible, but the poor encoding of irrelevant features with separate presentation makes it more difficult to observe.

Visual search is guided by representations of the target features
in working memory (WM; Bundesen, 1990; Duncan & Humphreys, 1989; Eimer, 2014; Schneider, 2013; Wolfe, 1994). For
instance, when we look for a red pen on a cluttered desk, we may
keep red and elongated in WM to guide attention to potential target objects. The question we address here is whether efficient
guidance requires a combined representation of these features in
WM or whether a separate representation is enough. Introspectively, the former idea rings true because we mostly look for
objects that combine two or more features. The alternative idea
that attention is guided by separate features is less intuitive. The
present research confirms the advantage of integrated over separate feature templates. However, we show that this advantage
results from the automatic encoding of features pertaining to an
object into WM. When encoding into WM is ensured, guidance by
separate features is equally effective.
Evidence for the object-based guidance of attention with integrated feature templates was provided by Foerster and Schneider
(2018, 2019, 2020). Foerster and Schneider asked their participants to memorize a target shape that was presented at the beginning of the trial. The target shape was randomly selected on each
trial to ensure that it was stored in WM and not in long-term memory (Carlisle et al., 2011; Woodman et al., 2013). After a retention
interval, the target shape was presented together with a distractor
shape, randomly to the left or right, and participants were asked to
look at the target shape. Saccades to one of the two objects
occurred with a latency of about 200 ms. The important manipulation in Foerster and Schneider’s experiments concerned the irrelevant color of the shapes (see also Figure 1). When the color of the
target shape was the same in the initial presentation and the saccadic choice display, saccadic responses were mostly correct and went to the target shape. In contrast, when the distractor was
shown in the initial color of the target shape, saccadic responses
were frequently wrong and went to the distractor. Thus, color
influenced responses although only shape was relevant, suggesting
that attention is automatically guided by all features of the object
acting as attentional template. The guidance by integrated feature
templates was observed not only for saccadic responses (Foerster
& Schneider, 2018), but also for perceptual judgments (Foerster &
Schneider, 2019) and mouse clicks (Kerzel & Andres, 2020). The
relevant and irrelevant dimensions (i.e., color and shape) can be
selected arbitrarily, but with the limitation that features on the relevant dimension are less discriminable than features on the irrelevant dimension (Foerster & Schneider, 2020).2 / 2

This passage is discussing the role of working memory (WM) in guiding attention during visual search tasks. The question being addressed is whether effective guidance requires a combined representation of the target features in WM or if a separate representation is enough. The authors provide evidence for the advantage of integrated over separate feature templates, but note that this advantage results from the automatic encoding of features pertaining to an object into WM. When encoding into WM is ensured, guidance by separate features is just as effective. The authors reference a series of experiments conducted by Foerster and Schneider to support their argument, where participants were asked to memorize a target shape and then look for it after a retention interval. The results showed that attention is guided by all features of an object, and that this guidance by integrated feature templates was observed for saccadic responses, perceptual judgments, and mouse clicks. The relevant and irrelevant dimensions (e.g. color and shape) can be selected arbitrarily, but the relevant dimension should have less discriminable features than the irrelevant dimension.

Summarise: Further support for the idea that both task-relevant and taskirrelevant features of an object guide attentional selection comes
from memory-based interference in visual search tasks (reviews in
Olivers et al., 2011; Soto et al., 2008). For instance, Gao et al.
(2016) presented a colored geometrical shape at the start of a trial.
Participants were instructed to memorize its color, which was
tested at the end of the trial. In contrast, the shape of the object
was task irrelevant. Between encoding and test of the color feature, participants performed a visual search task where they had to
indicate the orientation of the only tilted line among otherwise vertical lines. Each line was surrounded by a colored geometric
shape. In some search displays, one of the geometric shapes shared
the color or shape of the object presented at the start. The location
of the matching feature was not useful to locate the target because
the target was never shown at this location. Nonetheless, search
times increased when the surrounding color or shape matched the
object presented at the start. Importantly, memory-based interference occurred not only for the memorized color feature, but also
for the irrelevant shape feature, suggesting that all features of the
object were encoded into WM and guided attention away from the
target location (see also Soto & Humphreys, 2009). However, evidence for object-based memory interference was not always
observed. For instance, Olivers (2009) ran an experiment similar
to Gao et al. (2016), but only observed memory-based interference
for the relevant feature of the object presented at the start (see also
Sala & Courtney, 2009). Possibly, the discrepancy is due to the
longer interval between presentation of the object and the search
task in Olivers (2009) or Sala and Courtney (2009) compared with
Gao et al. (2016). With longer delays, the irrelevant information
may have decayed in WM (e.g., Logie et al., 2011) or may have
been recoded verbally (Olivers et al., 2006), which explains why
memory-based interference for the irrelevant feature was absent.
Alternatively, it may be that top-down control increased with
retention interval. Top-down control has been shown to decrease
interference from the irrelevant attribute (Han & Kim, 2009).

This passage provides further support for the idea that both task-relevant and task-irrelevant features of an object guide attentional selection in visual search tasks. The authors reference a study by Gao et al. (2016) where participants were instructed to memorize the color of a colored geometrical shape and then perform a visual search task. Search times increased when the surrounding color or shape matched the object presented at the start, suggesting that all features of the object were encoded into working memory (WM) and guided attention away from the target location. However, not all studies have found evidence for object-based memory interference, with one study observing memory-based interference only for the relevant feature of the object presented at the start. The discrepancy between studies may be due to the longer interval between presentation of the object and the search task, which may lead to decay of the irrelevant information in WM or recoding of the information verbally. It may also be due to increased top-down control, which has been shown to decrease interference from irrelevant attributes.

How SpecterX is different from DLPs (Data Leakage Prevention systems):
SpecterX is not a DLP solution. DLPs block data movement, SpecterX protects data movement.

When considering Data Leakage Prevention systems, they try to keep sensitive data from leaving the organization’s perimeter, with varying degrees of success. However, it’s hard teaching an automated system which data is sensitive and which isn’t, which often leads to many legitimate files being blocked (false-positives), reducing the confidence in these systems. But even when working correctly, the main problem is the approach - you can’t keep sensitive data from being shared outside of the organization - It’s part of the business’s day-to-day work. Companies have to share documents, plans, legal papers, and sometimes even their users’ data with external parties across their digital supply chain.
Moreover, it’s essential to know where it goes AFTER you shared it, and that is something that’s mostly missing in DLPs and other data protection solutions.

SpecterX doesn’t block data and doesn’t interfere with business operations. Instead, it follows the data wherever it goes, on any service, tool, device, and organization, and assures that only authorized users access it and only by the organization’s rules. We recognize the DLPs ability to categorize and label data is an essential part of keeping it safe. That’s why we integrate with DLPs, and other data protection solutions and use these abilities to enhance our data protection, even between a 4th and a 5th party (and so on) across the enterprise’s supply chain. That way, organizations get more value out of their already purchased data protection solution, extending their abilities beyond the organization’s perimeter. Moreover, SpecterX is already partnering with top DLP vendors to allow data to be classified and protected anywhere it travels.

In summary, SpecterX is a solution that protects data movement and provides visibility into where data goes after it is shared, while DLPs aim to prevent sensitive data from leaving the organization's perimeter by blocking data movement. However, this approach can lead to false-positives and reduced confidence in these systems. SpecterX integrates with DLPs to enhance their abilities, extend their protection beyond the organization's perimeter, and allow data to be classified and protected anywhere it travels. By doing so, organizations can get more value out of their already purchased data protection solution.

When an organization is ending a relationship with an employee, contractor, partner, or any external entity. IT and Security team need to make sure no sensitive data goes with them. Today, the total solutions exist in the offboarding use case, revoking access to its internal resources. But what about data that already left the organization’s infrastructure; to private email/cloud accounts, to someone else's hard drive, or even to an external corporation across the digital supply chain. This situation leaves the organization’s sensitive data vulnerable to security, compliance, and business risks as their data already located in someone else's hands without the ability to protect it. 

Using SpecterX IT and security teams can now revoke data access at its core level, regarding its location or infrastructure it is stored to ensure data will not leave the organization’s control. The SpecterX platform allows changing data access policies in several conditions and options, to meet the organization’s business process and compliance requirements.
What do companies risk with improper offboarding processes?

1. Data loss: When employees are laid off, the relationship between the employee and the organization can be soured. This could lead to former employees, who still have access to data, intentionally or unintentionally deleting or damaging files they know to be critical to the business. 

If access to your organization’s critical data isn’t properly revoked, data breach events are a real possibility. 

2. Compliance violations: Regulatory compliance frameworks are an extremely important part of the overall security posture of your organization. Former employees who still have access to sensitive data can leak or destroy it, which can lead to major compliance violations. When you look at HIPAA or GDPR as examples, the cost to your business for a violation can be substantial. For instance, GDPR fines can range up to 20 million euros or up to 4% of your global turnover.

3. Breaches of confidentiality: In the highly competitive world of business, companies can unscrupulously poach employees from competitors to get access to confidential contracts, business agreements and other proprietary knowledge. A former employee who still has access to the company’s confidential information can take it with them to a new employer. The consequences can be devastating. 

4. Data breach: The example given above details the real threat of another risk that comes from improperly offboarding an employee: stolen data. More than half of the employees surveyed by a Ponemon Institute study admitted to taking information from a former employer, and 40% admitted they intended to use it in a new job. Stolen data is a real security breach that has to be addressed by proper offboarding procedures and steps to prevent data exfiltration.

An employee sends a “secure message” containing sensitive data to a supplier. Supplier gets an email with a link to a “secure environment”. An OTP is generated to the external party in order to authenticate to the “Secure Environment”. An authorization process is validating external party watch the employee message under the organization’s policy. External party reply to the message and an email sent to the employee contains the external party’s response. The data is deleted from the secure environment.
Human Error Prevention
Sending the wrong file to the wrong entity with the ability to revoke access after data has been downloaded / opened in a remote location.
Moreover, you will have complete visibility of any data access and usage.

Supply Chain Management
Big insurance and medical organizations handle many lawsuits every year, and through a massive digital supply chain of multiple law firms, insurance and medical institutions, advisors, etc’. Each one works differently, with their preference for tools and workflows. This is especially an issue when the sending organization and the external parties use different tools by different providers (for example, Microsoft vs. Google), forcing them to abandon their configured environment and work insecurely. This makes sharing data securely nearly impossible and opens the supply chain to data theft.

But this is only the beginning. These law firms don’t work alone; they need to share the data onward with consultants, specialists, advisors, and other professionals. As this digital-supply-chain grows, the risk of a data breach becomes exponentially more likely.
This is precisely the case with one of our clients, which estimates his yearly losses from data-breaches to ongoing lawsuits in the millions every year.

Title: The Curse of Nutmeg

Description: Nutmeg, once a human wizard, was cursed by a coven of hags and turned into a Russian Blue cat. As she gradually loses her sense of human self, she desires to regain her true form and confront the hags responsible for her transformation. An adventure to find the coven, lift the curse, and possibly make new allies along the way.

Dangers:

1. The Watchful Monster
A sentient monster, perhaps a Displacer Beast, was sent by the coven to ensure Nutmeg remains cursed and to bring her back if she tries to break it. This monster will try to hinder her progress, revealing itself only when necessary.

Grim Portents:

* Mysterious signs of being watched or followed.
* The monster sabotages the party's efforts to find the coven.
* The monster reveals itself and tries to capture Nutmeg.

Impending Doom: Nutmeg is captured and returned to the coven, losing her chance to regain her humanity.

1. The Hag's Deceit
The coven is aware that Nutmeg seeks a way to break the curse and uses deception to lure her into their grasp.

Grim Portents:

* The party receives false information about a cure for Nutmeg's curse.
* Nutmeg encounters an NPC claiming to have the knowledge or power to help her, but with ulterior motives.
* The party is lured into a trap set by the hags.

Impending Doom: The hags ensnare Nutmeg and the party, cementing Nutmeg's curse and causing further harm to the group.

Stakes:

1. Will Nutmeg find a way to lift the curse and regain her human form?
2. How will Nutmeg and the party deal with the Watchful Monster?
3. Can Nutmeg and the party discern the truth amidst the hag's deceit?
4. If Nutmeg confronts the coven, what will be the outcome?

This modular adventure front can be integrated into your main campaign. You can introduce the Watchful Monster and the Hag's Deceit as background threats while the party focuses on other objectives. When the time is right, these dangers can take center stage, pushing Nutmeg and the party to confront the coven of hags and seek a way to lift the curse.

The formula w\_i = w\_i \* exp(-alpha \* y\_i \* h(x\_i)) / Z is used to adjust the weights of the training examples in AdaBoost (Adaptive Boosting), a popular boosting algorithm in machine learning.

Here's a brief explanation of each term in the formula:

* w\_i: The weight of training example i.
* alpha: A parameter that controls the contribution of each model to the final prediction. Higher values of alpha give more weight to the current model, while lower values give more weight to previous models.
* y\_i: The true label of training example i.
* h(x\_i): The prediction of the previous model on training example i.
* Z: A normalization factor that ensures the weights sum to one.

The term exp(-alpha \* y\_i \* h(x\_i)) can be thought of as a measure of how much the current model contributes to the error of training example i. If the current model predicts the correct label for example i (i.e., y\_i \* h(x\_i) > 0), then this term will be close to zero, and the weight of example i will remain the same. However, if the current model predicts the wrong label for example i (i.e., y\_i \* h(x\_i) < 0), then this term will be greater than one, and the weight of example i will be increased.

The normalization factor Z is used to ensure that the weights sum to one, which is necessary for the weights to be interpretable as a probability distribution. The formula for Z depends on the sum of the weights and the values of alpha, y\_i, and h(x\_i) for each example in the training set.

The idea behind this weight update formula is to give more weight to the examples that are misclassified by the previous model, so that the next model will focus more on those examples and try to correct the errors of the previous model. This iterative process of adjusting the weights and training new models leads to improved performance over time, and is the key idea behind AdaBoost and many other boosting algorithms.

In boosting, the predictions of the individual models are combined to obtain a final prediction. The specific method used to combine the models depends on the boosting algorithm being used and the problem being solved.

Here are a few common methods for combining the predictions of the models in boosting:

1. Weighted majority voting: In this method, each model is assigned a weight based on its performance on the training set. The final prediction is obtained by taking a weighted majority vote of the predictions of the individual models, where the weights are proportional to the performance of the models.
2. Simple average: In this method, the predictions of the individual models are averaged to obtain a final prediction. This method is often used in regression problems, where the goal is to predict a continuous variable.
3. Stacking: In this method, the predictions of the individual models are used as input features to a new model, which learns to combine the predictions of the individual models. This method can be effective for complex problems where simple combinations of the models may not be sufficient.

The choice of method for combining the models depends on the specific problem being solved and the characteristics of the individual models. In practice, different methods may be compared using cross-validation or other methods to determine the best approach for a given problem.

In this method, each model is assigned a weight based on its performance on the training set, and the final prediction is obtained by taking a weighted majority vote of the predictions of the individual models.

Here's an example of how to use weighted majority voting in Python:
```python

from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score

# Define the models to be combined
model1 = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=1)
model2 = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=3)
model3 = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=5)

# Train each model on the training set
model1.fit(X_train, y_train)
model2.fit(X_train, y_train)
model3.fit(X_train, y_train)

# Compute the accuracy of each model on the training set
acc1 = accuracy_score(y_train, model1.predict(X_train))
acc2 = accuracy_score(y_train, model2.predict(X_train))
acc3 = accuracy_score(y_train, model3.predict(X_train))

# Assign weights to each model based on their accuracy
total_acc = acc1 + acc2 + acc3
weights = [acc1/total_acc, acc2/total_acc, acc3/total_acc]

# Make predictions on the test set using each model
pred1 = model1.predict(X_test)
pred2 = model2.predict(X_test)
pred3 = model3.predict(X_test)

# Combine the predictions of the models using weighted majority voting
final_pred = [int(pred1[i]*weights[0] + pred2[i]*weights[1] + pred3[i]*weights[2] >= 0.5) for i in range(len(X_test))]

# Compute the accuracy of the final prediction
accuracy = accuracy_score(y_test, final_pred)
```
In this example, we first define three decision tree classifiers with different maximum depths. We then train each model on the training set and compute its accuracy on the training set. We assign weights to each model based on its accuracy, and use the weights to combine the predictions of the models using weighted majority voting. Finally, we compute the accuracy of the final prediction on the test set.

Note that the weights assigned to each model can be adjusted based on various factors, such as the complexity of the model, the size of the training set, or the importance of different features. Repudiation of a contract occurs when a party to the contract shows an unwillingness or inability to perform substantial obligations under the contract. This conduct is often referred to as renunciation. For instance, if a builder tells a homeowner that they will not complete work on the agreed completion date or that they will not complete work as agreed, then they may be repudiating the contract.

Contract Repudiation is considered a breach of contract because it goes against the fundamental principle of a contract, which is to carry out the agreed terms. When a party repudiates a contract, they are not fulfilling their contractual obligations.

As a result, the other party is entitled to terminate the contract and seek damages for any losses suffered.

Repudiation of contract is not the same as termination, but it can lead to termination. Termination can occur through contractual provisions or the common law right of termination for repudiation.

A retrospective, also known as a retro, is a meeting that is held at the end of an iteration in agile software development. It is a time for the team to reflect on their work and identify areas for improvement. A retro template is a structured format or framework that guides the team through the process of conducting a retro.

Here are some examples of retro templates that teams can use:

* Start, Stop, Continue: This template involves the team discussing what they should start doing, stop doing, and continue doing in order to improve their processes and outcomes.
* Mad, Sad, Glad: This template involves the team sharing what made them mad, sad, or glad during the iteration. This can help the team identify and address negative experiences, as well as celebrate positive ones.
* 4Ls: This template involves the team discussing what they Learned, Liked, Lacked, and Longed for during the iteration. This can help the team identify what worked well and what didn't, and generate ideas for improvement.
* Plus, Delta: This template involves the team discussing what they did well (the Plus) and what they could improve on (the Delta) during the iteration. This can help the team focus on both their strengths and areas for improvement.

These are just a few examples of retro templates that teams can use. There are many other templates available, and teams can also create their own custom templates to suit their specific needs and preferences.

The book is structured around twenty key themes that Montaigne addressed in his work, and it offers an accessible and engaging interpretation of his thoughts. Here are some major takeaways from the book:

1. Embrace the complexity of human nature: Montaigne believed in accepting and understanding the full range of human emotions, thoughts, and behaviors. He encouraged his readers to delve into their own psyches and appreciate their unique experiences.
2. Be skeptical and question everything: Montaigne was a proponent of skepticism and often questioned conventional wisdom. He urged readers to question their own beliefs and assumptions, as well as those of others, to arrive at a deeper understanding of the world.
3. Cultivate self-awareness: One of Montaigne's most enduring contributions to philosophy is his emphasis on introspection and self-awareness. He believed that understanding oneself was crucial to living a good life and encouraged a constant examination of one's thoughts and actions.
4. Accept uncertainty: Montaigne recognized that life is full of uncertainties and ambiguities. Instead of despairing over this fact, he suggested embracing it as a natural part of the human experience and learning to navigate it with grace and humility.
5. Enjoy the present moment: Montaigne advocated for living in the present and appreciating the simple pleasures of life. He believed that happiness could be found in everyday experiences, like spending time with friends and family or enjoying a good meal.
6. Practice empathy and understanding: Montaigne emphasized the importance of empathy and understanding in human relationships. He believed that by putting ourselves in others' shoes, we can foster greater compassion and tolerance.
7. Develop a personal philosophy: Montaigne's essays were a form of self-exploration and a way for him to develop his own personal philosophy. Bakewell encourages readers to engage in a similar process, using Montaigne's work as a guide and inspiration for discovering their own values and principles.
8. Embrace life's contradictions: Montaigne's writing often reflects his acceptance of life's contradictions and paradoxes. He believed that embracing these complexities, rather than trying to resolve them, is a more authentic and fulfilling way to live.
9. Cultivate resilience: Montaigne's life was marked by personal loss and political turmoil, but he managed to maintain a sense of equanimity throughout. Bakewell suggests that cultivating resilience and adaptability is essential for navigating the challenges of life.

Great! Asymmetric cryptography, also known as public-key cryptography, is a type of encryption that uses two different keys to encrypt and decrypt data. One key, called the public key, is used to encrypt the data, while the other key, called the private key, is used to decrypt it.

Here's a simple asymmetric cipher that you can use to encrypt a string of text:

1. Choose two large prime numbers, p and q, and calculate their product n = p\*q.
2. Calculate Euler's totient function phi(n) = (p-1)\*(q-1).
3. Choose a number e that is relatively prime to phi(n), i.e., the greatest common divisor of e and phi(n) is 1. The number e is your public key.
4. Calculate the modular multiplicative inverse d of e modulo phi(n), i.e., d is the number such that (d\*e) mod phi(n) = 1. The number d is your private key.
5. To encrypt a message M, convert it to a number m using some fixed encoding (e.g., ASCII or Unicode), then compute the ciphertext C = m^e mod n.
6. To decrypt the ciphertext C, compute the plaintext m = C^d mod n, then convert it back to the original message using the same encoding.

Here's an example of how to use this cipher to encrypt the message "Hello, world!":

1. Choose two large prime numbers, p = 23 and q = 37, and calculate their product n = p\*q = 851.
2. Calculate Euler's totient function phi(n) = (p-1)\*(q-1) = 792.
3. Choose a number e that is relatively prime to phi(n). Let's choose e = 7. Therefore, our public key is (7, 851).
4. Calculate the modular multiplicative inverse d of e modulo phi(n). We can use the Extended Euclidean Algorithm to compute d = 535. Therefore, our private key is (535, 851).
5. Convert the message "Hello, world!" to a number using ASCII encoding. We get m = 72 101 108 108 111 44 32 119 111 114 108 100 33.
6. Encrypt the message by computing C = m^e mod n = 702 704 300 280 441 95 693 36 441 137 184 143 137 mod 851. The ciphertext is C = 456.
7. To decrypt the ciphertext, compute the plaintext m = C^d mod n = 72 101 108 108 111 44 32 119 111 114 108 100 33. Convert the plaintext back to the original message using ASCII encoding. We get the message "Hello, world!".

Note that this is a very basic example of an asymmetric cipher and is not suitable for secure communication as it has many vulnerabilities. In practice, asymmetric ciphers are much more complex and require significant expertise to design and implement securely.

Prime numbers are relevant in asymmetric cryptography because the security of the algorithm relies on the difficulty of factoring large numbers into their prime factors.

In the RSA encryption algorithm, for example, the security of the encryption scheme depends on the fact that it is computationally infeasible to factor a large composite number into its two prime factors. The two large prime numbers are used to generate the public and private keys, and the security of the encryption scheme is based on the fact that it is extremely difficult to compute the private key from the public key without knowing the two prime factors.

If you were to use non-prime numbers for generating your keys, it would be much easier for an attacker to factor the modulus (the product of the two non-prime numbers) and compute the private key from the public key. This would render the encryption scheme vulnerable to attacks.

Therefore, using prime numbers in asymmetric cryptography is essential to ensure the security of the encryption scheme.

In a man-in-the-middle attack, an attacker intercepts communication between a website and a user's browser, and can steal sensitive information or modify the communication. HSTS helps prevent this by telling the user's browser to only communicate with the website using a secure connection (HTTPS), and never to allow communication using an insecure connection (HTTP).

Think of a strong front door as a way to keep intruders out of a house. Once the front door is locked, intruders cannot enter the house, even if they try to trick the resident into opening the door for them. Similarly, once HSTS is implemented on a website, the user's browser will not allow communication with the website using an insecure connection, even if an attacker tries to trick the user into visiting a fake version of the website.

In this analogy, the house represents a website, the front door represents the user's browser, and the strong front door represents HSTS. By implementing HSTS, website owners can help keep their website and their users' information safe from attackers.

As a union leader preparing for the renewal of a collective bargaining agreement, here are some steps you can take to prepare:

1. Review the Current Agreement: Take a thorough review of the existing collective bargaining agreement (CBA). Make note of any outstanding issues or concerns that need to be addressed, and any successes or wins that you would like to maintain.
2. Survey Members: Conduct a survey or hold meetings with union members to get a better understanding of their needs and priorities for the upcoming CBA negotiations. This information will be useful in developing your bargaining goals.
3. Establish Bargaining Goals: Based on the feedback received from union members and your own review of the current CBA, establish a list of bargaining goals. Prioritize these goals based on their importance to union members and the feasibility of achieving them.
4. Develop a Bargaining Strategy: Once you have established bargaining goals, develop a strategy for achieving them. This may involve determining which issues to address first, deciding on bargaining tactics and timelines, and identifying any potential roadblocks or obstacles.
5. Research Industry Standards: Research current industry standards and trends in collective bargaining agreements in your field. This will help you determine what is reasonable to ask for and what is not.
6. Build Solidarity: Building solidarity with other unions in your industry or region can be a powerful bargaining tool. Consider joining forces with other unions to negotiate collective bargaining agreements that benefit all workers in the industry.
7. Anticipate Management Tactics: Consider the tactics management may use during negotiations and prepare counter-arguments and strategies for dealing with them.
8. Keep Members Informed: Throughout the bargaining process, keep union members informed of any progress or setbacks. This will help maintain morale and build solidarity.
9. Develop an Action Plan: If negotiations break down, have an action plan in place. This may include a strike, picketing, or other forms of labor action.

By taking these steps, you can prepare for collective bargaining negotiations and increase the likelihood of achieving your goals.

What is the difference between authentization and authorization?

Authentication and authorization are two different concepts in the context of computer security.

Authentication refers to the process of verifying the identity of a user or system, typically by requiring a username and password. The goal is to ensure that the user or system accessing a resource is who they claim to be.

Authorization, on the other hand, refers to the process of granting or denying access to a resource based on the permissions associated with the authenticated user or system. Authorization determines whether an authenticated user has the necessary permissions to access a particular resource or perform a particular action.

In simple terms, authentication is about verifying identity, while authorization is about determining what a user or system is allowed to do once their identity has been established.

What is API token; what is Oauth2.0?

API Token and OAuth 2.0 are both authentication mechanisms used in APIs to grant access to resources.

API Token is a unique identifier that is issued by an API provider to a client application that allows the client to access the API. The token is a string of characters that is sent along with each API request to identify the client and grant access to specific resources. The API token is a form of authentication that is typically used for simple API integrations where only one client application needs to access the API.

OAuth 2.0, on the other hand, is a more secure authentication mechanism that allows a user to grant a third-party application access to their resources on a server, without sharing their credentials. OAuth 2.0 enables users to authenticate using their social media or other online accounts. For example, a user can use their Google account to sign in to another application without having to create a new account. OAuth 2.0 allows clients to be granted access to specific resources for a limited time, known as access tokens, without exposing the user's credentials to the client.

In summary, API tokens are used to identify the client making the API request, while OAuth 2.0 is a more secure authentication mechanism that allows users to grant third-party applications access to their resources without exposing their credentials.

Step ten: often we get stuck, arguing with the patient, or more subtly asking the patient not to do what he or she is doing. That is, we are resisting the patient’s resistance. What's the significance of square footage in real estate? Why are prices often normalized by square footage?

Square footage is a significant factor in real estate because it serves as a standardized measurement of the size of a property, allowing for easier comparison between different properties. In both residential and commercial real estate, the size of a property is one of the primary determinants of its value, along with location, condition, and other features. By normalizing prices by square footage, buyers and sellers can more easily compare properties and assess their relative value.

Here are some reasons why prices are often normalized by square footage in real estate:

1. Comparability: Normalizing prices by square footage allows potential buyers and sellers to easily compare properties on a per-square-foot basis. This helps them determine whether a property is priced fairly and enables them to make informed decisions.
2. Market trends: Analyzing the price per square foot of properties sold in a particular area over time can help identify market trends and patterns, such as whether property values are increasing, decreasing, or remaining stable.
3. Appraisal and valuation: Square footage is often used by appraisers and real estate professionals to estimate the market value of a property. By comparing the price per square foot of similar properties that have recently sold in the same area, they can establish a reasonable range for the property's value.
4. Space requirements: Square footage is a useful metric for buyers and tenants to assess whether a property meets their space requirements. For example, a family may need a certain amount of square footage to accommodate their belongings and ensure a comfortable living environment.
5. Efficiency and cost analysis: Investors and property managers can use the price per square foot to analyze the efficiency and profitability of a property. By comparing the cost per square foot with rental income or other returns, they can determine if the property is a worthwhile investment.

In conclusion, normalizing prices by square footage in real estate helps facilitate more accurate comparisons, valuations, and analyses. It is a widely recognized and essential metric in the industry, helping both buyers and sellers make more informed decisions.
Why square footage instead of lot size?

While lot size is an important factor in real estate, square footage is used more commonly as a primary comparison metric for several reasons:

1. Living space: Square footage refers to the actual living or usable space within a property, which is a primary concern for most buyers and renters. It directly impacts the level of comfort, functionality, and the ability to accommodate belongings and furniture. Lot size, on the other hand, represents the overall land area of a property, which may include outdoor spaces that are not directly related to the living experience.
2. Consistency: Square footage is a consistent measure that applies to both interior and exterior spaces, whereas lot size may vary significantly between properties due to factors such as shape, topography, and landscaping. Square footage offers a standardized way to compare properties based on the amount of usable space they provide.
3. Applicability: Square footage is a relevant metric for both residential and commercial properties, as it reflects the available living or working space in both contexts. Lot size, however, may be less relevant for certain types of commercial properties where the focus is on interior space and functionality rather than the outdoor area.
4. Amenities and property features: Square footage includes the space occupied by various amenities and property features, such as bedrooms, bathrooms, living areas, and kitchen spaces. These features have a direct impact on the comfort and functionality of a property and are often of greater concern to buyers and renters than the size of the lot.
5. Marketability: Properties are often marketed and promoted based on their square footage because it is a more tangible and relatable metric for potential buyers and renters. Lot size, while important, may not be as easily understood or visualized, especially for those who are not familiar with real estate measurements.

That said, lot size is still an important consideration in real estate, particularly for those who value outdoor space, potential for expansion, or privacy. Buyers and investors should consider both square footage and lot size, along with other factors, to make well-informed decisions about a property's suitability and value.
In cases where the land is more valuable than the home, would lot size be a better normalized metric for price?

Yes, in cases where the land value is more significant than the value of the structure on it, lot size can be a more appropriate normalized metric for price comparison. This can occur in certain situations, such as:

1. Redevelopment potential: In areas with high demand for new development, the land's value may be more important than the existing structure. Developers may be more interested in the lot size to determine the potential for building new residential or commercial projects.
2. Scarcity of land: In locations where land is scarce or highly sought after, such as prime urban or waterfront areas, lot size can be a more important factor in determining the property's value. In these cases, the land itself is considered a premium asset.
3. Agricultural or recreational uses: When purchasing property for agricultural or recreational purposes, buyers may prioritize lot size over the structure's square footage. In these cases, the land's usability and potential for farming, livestock, or recreational activities are more important than the home or buildings on the property.
4. Zoning regulations: If zoning regulations allow for significant expansion, subdivision, or changes in land use, the lot size can be more important than the existing structure's size. In such cases, the land's potential for future development or expansion can drive its value.
5. Tear-downs or major renovations: When a property's structure is in poor condition, outdated, or not suited for the buyer's needs, the lot size may become more relevant. Buyers or investors may plan to demolish the existing structure and rebuild a new home or building, making the land's size and potential more significant than the current structure.

In these situations, normalizing price by lot size can provide a better basis for comparison and evaluation of a property's value. However, it's essential to consider various factors, such as location, zoning, and local market conditions, when making decisions based on lot size.

SUMMARISE: "Interactions in the workforce play an important role in
team performance and productivity [1], [2]. For example,
informal inter-team interactions have been shown to be an
important trait of successful teams [3]. Work interactions can
also influence the design of physical spaces [4] or help in
developing an understanding of disease spreading [5], [6].
Researchers have relied on surveys and observations for years
to gather data about these phenomena. However, the cost of
observations is high as they usually involve long hours of
monitoring. They might also not scale to many participants
and can therefore only be applied to phenomena restricted
temporally. Surveys instead scale better but offer a much
coarser grained view as people might forget to report [7].
Usually two contrasting needs are faced when trying to
capture such interactions automatically: (1) the need to collect
accurate and reliable data and (2) the need to have large
deployments to get a clearer picture of human behaviour.
Existing solutions usually tend to tackle more one problem
or the other. Bluetooth-based systems for example can rely
on widespread adoption but are usually power hungry and do
not offer fine grained data [8], [9], [10], [6]. On the other
hand, systems based on custom built devices can provide
fine granularity but require dedicated hardware which hinder
adoption [11], [12], [13]. The recent interest in wearable
devices [14] has brought us to question if those devices are
able to fulfill both needs. In particular we directed our attention
towards Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) which is included in all
current wearables. We envision an interaction sensing system
that can be easily installed on a wearable device like a smart
watch thus extending its functionality to interaction sensing
and offering widespread adoption. However, before this can
become a reality there are fundamental questions which need
answers. Namely: How accurate could BLE proximity detection
be? What could be the expected lifetime of this system
on an off-the-shelf device? How can it be employed for social
interaction sensing and space occupancy monitoring?
In this work, we analyse the potential of BLE to monitor
people proximity as first step towards a social interaction
sensing system. The objective is to asses its capabilities, first
by analysing its parameters and their impact on both accuracy
and power consumption, and then, from a practical perspective,
with a large user study in a real workplace.
Current hardware, available in modern wearables and smart
watches, offers the key functionality for proximity detection:
the ability to detect nearby devices and be detected by them
by alternating between transmitting and scanning. While the
manufactures have recently updated device firmwares and
software stacks to support this kind of behaviour there are still
several limitations that prevent an accurate study of all the key
factors involved in proximity monitoring. In particular, mobile
operating systems do not allow the application developer to
freely control all the BLE parameters. Thus, we build and use
a custom made wearable prototype in which we are in control
of all parameters. This allows us to study in detail the interplay
of all the BLE parameters and their impact on power consumption.
Using our prototype we collected proximity traces
in a commercial organisation with 25 participants to extend
our analysis to a real world scenario and to not limit ourself
only to lab experiments. We were then able, through data
post-processing, to investigate the achievable performances
if our system were to run on off-the-shelf wearable devices
and understand their strengths and weaknesses. This led us
to the important conclusion that large scale proximity studies
are viable, even at the accuracy level required by domain
scientists, with off-the-shelf devices.
To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study of
BLE radios on a wearable platform for proximity monitoring
which provides useful insights for social interaction sensing
applications. This paper also offers guidance to OS developers
and manufacturers on the impact of the limitations of their
APIs and informs application developers on the flexibility of
off-the-shelf wearables. Our contributions are:
\_ a detailed analysis of BLE parameters that play a central
role in proximity detection;
\_ the first analysis of BLE capabilities and limitations on
commercial wearable devices (Android Wear and Tizen);
\_ an extensive experimental validation with lab experiments
and a longitudinal user study with 25 participants in an
office environment. We confirm the BLE suitability for
accurate proximity monitoring with 97% accuracy at 10
seconds granularity. Ground truth observation for around
19 hours was performed to support our evaluation.
\_ a discussion on the restrictions imposed by OS developers
on the use of BLE for proximity detection.
II. MOTIVATION AND RELATED WORK
Accurate human proximity detection has the potential to
influence many different disciplines (e.g., social science, architecture
and health). Proximity detection often depends on
the phenomena under observation: in certain cases only short
events with a very small distance between the participants areA
relevant (e.g., when certain virus spreading is considered), in
others, only prolonged interactions that would give individuals
a chance to have meaningful conversations are pertinent.
The specific scenario considered for this paper is the one
that takes into consideration office based social interactions.
In such setting, serendipitous interactions, where, say, a user
glances from an office doorway, might be meaningful and
indicative of productivity [3], [15]. This is, of course, in
addition to prolonged and repeated interactions.
The detection of fairly long lived interaction (of the order of
several tens of seconds) has been accomplished by technology
reasonably successfully. Bluetooth Classic has often been at
the basis of these platforms mainly due to its availability on
consumer devices, which makes it extremely suitable to large
deployments [8], [6], [16]. However, several works [9], [10]
have tried to improve the temporal and spatial granularity of
traces collected with Bluetooth Classic. In fact, Bluetooth’s
main drawbacks reside in the high power consumption and
low granularity of the traces. Usually, it is sampled every few
minutes [8], [16] to avoid draining the battery too quickly and
the range of transmission is around 10m [6].
Other technologies have also been proposed, for instance,
RFID [17], Zigbee radio [18], infrared sensors [12] and hybrid
approaches with radio and ultrasound sensors [13]. These
devices offer better performance (e.g. temporal granularity
from 20s to 2s with still reasonable battery consumption) but
are not suitable for wide scale and long term adoption because
they rely on dedicated hardware which needs to be deployed
just for the purpose of the study. In fact, problems have been
reported with the usability of these devices [7].
Few works have used specifically BLE to collect data
about human behaviour. Townsend et al. tested 4 different
smartphones to asses if they could detect each other using
BLE [19]. Boonstra et al. deployed an Android and iOS
app to 14 participants for a period of one working week to
collect data about social contacts [20]. However, the authors
offered a limited evaluation of their system by using only two
meetings during the study period to validate their methodology
and they did not collect participants’ locations, which is a
valuable piece of information when studying social dynamics.
Other works instead have used simple wearable BLE tags,
capable of transmitting only, to study mobility patterns of
large gatherings [21], [22]. Radhakrishnan et al. have recently
analysed BLE characteristics on Android mobile phones for
indoor localisation [23]. They implemented a BLE-like duty
cycling on top of the Android BLE stack which already
performs duty cycling in accordance to the BLE specification.
Here we offer instead an analysis of the low level BLE
parameters (as defined in the standard) to understand if BLE
can be employed to collect fine grained and accurate encounter
traces. We then analyse if the approach could be adopted on
commercial wearable devices to free proximity-based systems
from the need for custom devices, which is usually one of
the limiting factors of long term studies. Additionally, the
availability of our prototype allowed us to test the impact of
these parameters on a large scale deployment."

The case of Video Master v. Nishi Productions dealt with the issue of copyright infringement in the film industry. The Plaintiff claimed that the sole and exclusive video copyrights in a cinematographic film (Bees Saal Baad) were assigned to it under an agreement by the producer of the film, the Defendant. It alleged that the Defendant had entered into an agreement with another distributor, whereby a copy of the film was given to them, which in turn was used to make cassettes which were to be used for satellite TV transmission. Thus, a violation of the copyright of the Plaintiff was alleged.

The court held that copyrights in Cable TV rights and satellite broadcasting rights are two different rights under the Copyright Act, which can exist in different persons without infringing the copyright of each other. By receiving satellite signals on a dish antenna owned/maintained by Cable TV operator or private party and by relaying signals through the media of Cable to the viewers, there was no violation of the exclusive video copyright of the Plaintiff.

In this case, the court ruled that the defendant did not infringe the plaintiff's copyright by providing the film to a third party for satellite transmission, as the copyrights in cable TV rights and satellite broadcasting rights are different rights and can exist independently of each other.

communication depends essentially on the persons receiving the communication. It they can
be characterized as the public or a portion of the public, the communication is to the case laid
down that showing a film on a cable television network was a broadcast of the film to the

through a dish antenna to which their television sets are connected, are either residents of
Apartments in a building which has such a network or they may be residents of a locality
which is covered by this facility. A number of houses - both private homes and public places -
may avail of this facility. As the viewers are not members of one family or their guests and do
not have any homogeneity, they are the members of public. (3) Therefore communication of a

the copyright in the film.
Thus one would find that the elaboration of the Broadcaster’s rights, despite their statutory

Linux is a free and open-source operating system that is based on the Unix operating system. It is widely used for servers, desktop computers, and mobile devices. Some of the key features of Linux include:

* Command-line interface: Linux uses a command-line interface (CLI) for interacting with the operating system. Users can enter commands to perform tasks such as navigating the file system, managing files and directories, and running programs.
* File system: Linux uses a hierarchical file system, with the root directory represented as '/'. Users can navigate through the file system using commands such as 'cd' (change directory) and 'ls' (list files and directories).
* Package management: Linux uses package managers to install, update, and manage software packages. Popular package managers include apt (for Debian-based distributions) and yum (for Red Hat-based distributions).
* Users and permissions: Linux has a robust system for managing users and permissions. Each user has a unique username and a UID (user ID) and GID (group ID). Users can be assigned different levels of access to files and directories based on their UID and GID.
* Shells: Linux uses shells, which are command-line interpreters, to accept and execute commands. The most common shell on Linux is the Bash (Bourne Again Shell), but others include Zsh and Tcsh.
* Scripting: Linux supports scripting with various languages like Bash, Python, and Perl, which can automate repetitive tasks and perform complex operations.
* Open-source: Linux is open-source, meaning that its source code is available for anyone to view, modify, and distribute. This allows for a large and active community of developers and users who contribute to the development and improvement of the operating system.

In summary, Linux is a free and open-source operating system that is widely used for servers, desktop computers, and mobile devices, It is based on the Unix operating system and uses a command-line interface, a hierarchical file system, package management, robust user and permission system, shells and scripting languages, and it has an active open-source community.

Sure! Here's how you can compare the two sets of data and determine how many responses are in both sets and how many are unique to each set using R:

1. Import the data from the first round and the second round into R as separate data frames. Let's call them `data1` and `data2`, respectively.
2. Use the `intersect()` function to find the common responses between the two sets of data:
```bash
common_responses <- intersect(data1$Name, data2$Name)
```
This will give you a vector of the names that appear in both `data1` and `data2`.

1. Use the `setdiff()` function to find the unique responses in each set:
```bash
unique_responses1 <- setdiff(data1$Name, data2$Name)
unique_responses2 <- setdiff(data2$Name, data1$Name)
```
This will give you two vectors of the names that appear only in `data1` or only in `data2`, respectively.

1. To check the number of common responses, use the `length()` function:
```r
num_common_responses <- length(common_responses)
```
This will give you the number of responses that appear in both `data1` and `data2`.

1. To check the number of unique responses in each set, use the `length()` function again:
```r
num_unique_responses1 <- length(unique_responses1)
num_unique_responses2 <- length(unique_responses2)
```
This will give you the number of responses that appear only in `data1` or only in `data2`, respectively.

into:

To transform the given lines using regular expressions and remove the leading zeros and whitespace, you can use the following pattern:
```ruby
^0+\s*(\w+)$
```
And replace with the capture group 1 (`$1`) which matches the alphabets.

Here's an example in Python:
```python
import re

lines = ['0003 AB', '0568 FD']

for line in lines:
    result = re.sub(r'^0+\s*(\w+)$', r'\1', line)
    print(result)
```
Output:
```
AB
FD
```
In the regular expression pattern, `^` matches the start of the string, `0+` matches one or more zeros, `\s*` matches zero or more whitespace characters, and `(\w+)` matches one or more word characters (letters, digits, or underscores) and captures them in a group. `$` matches the end of the string. The `r'\1'` replacement string references the first capture group.

Hilton, a century-old multinational hospitality company, was founded by Conrad Hilton in 1919. Hilton hotels, headquartered in Tysons Corner, Virginia, has 12 brands and 5,500 hotels across 110 countries. Of the 12 brands, Hilton hotels have three luxury brands: Conrad Hotels and Resorts, the Waldorf Astoria, and Tempo hotels (Hotel Tech Report, 2017). These three luxury brands exist on five continents with 100+ luxury properties across the globe (Brettell, 2022). With this scale, Hilton's consumer base is scattered around the world. Therefore, the company required convenient communication channels to treat its luxury consumers with royalty. With the increasing popularity of digital media amongst consumers, Hilton consumers are also moving towards digital media, especially Twitter, to reach, connect, request, and ask for services from the company. Hilton, therefore, needed a way to keep in touch with consumers in real time. Hence, they devised a social listening strategy that would keep them alert and ready to respond whenever, wherever, to whomever.

Hilton's Social Media Listening Strategy

Hilton Hotels receive 1.5K Twitter mentions daily. Most of these 1.5k tweets carry positive sentiments and are associated with marketing offers from travel and tourism companies, news channels, and Hiltons' consumers sharing pictures and tagging the location. While these posts may seem to require less of the brand's attention and response. However, Hilton's social media team prioritizes addressing any conversation or mention, whether positive or negative, to get a response within a few hours.

On an average, Hilton Hotels responds to 3.3 tweets per hour, with a 37.3-minute average time between a tweet and a response (Bredava, 2018). This is much quicker than the industry average of 10 hours and consumers' expected wait time of four hours. Hence, in this manner, Hilton hotel ensures delivering royal and luxury services to consumers by listening and responding to them in time. This real-time discussion between the brand and the consumers elevates the consumer experience and provides them with a moment of happiness. However, to deliver this moment of happiness to consumers, Hilton's social media team works round the clock to respond and engage with consumers in real-time. In this regard, the Social Business Lead and Strategist at Hilton Hotels said, "We took a different approach than a lot of companies. We want to help our guests no matter how they come to us. No matter how they want help — in the app, at the front desk, or on Twitter. We are there where they want us."

Hence, Hilton houses their guest service center along with its call centre. This enables the service team to monitor the calls and tweets round the clock and get in touch with the required team – call center or social media team within 30 minutes of a mention to revert to the guests. Furthermore, to enable tapping and addressing of untagged mentions, Hilton hotels use hashtags to monitor such tweets and provide timely responses to its consumers. This strategy of Hilton is extremely unique and the brand is applauded for their dedication towards providing luxury consumer services. "We want to be available to the customer wherever they are. It just comes down to customer preference, whether they want to tweet our main account or one of our hotels, or don't @ us at all — and monitoring it all," remarks Sain-Dieguez.

```vb
Sub AddNumbers()
```

could you write a macro that would copy each row from workbook, then create microsoft word file and paste that row from excel each on new page?

Certainly! Here's an example macro that will copy each row from an Excel workbook and paste it into a new Microsoft Word file, with each row on a new page:
```vb
Sub CopyRowsToWord()
    Dim wb As Workbook
    Dim ws As Worksheet
    Dim wrdApp As Word.Application
    Dim wrdDoc As Word.Document
    Dim i As Long
    
    ' Set up the Excel and Word objects
    Set wb = ThisWorkbook
    Set ws = wb.Worksheets("Sheet1") ' Change "Sheet1" to the name of your worksheet
    Set wrdApp = CreateObject("Word.Application")
    wrdApp.Visible = True ' Set to False if you don't want Word to be visible
    Set wrdDoc = wrdApp.Documents.Add
    
    ' Loop through each row in the worksheet and copy the data to Word
    For i = 1 To ws.UsedRange.Rows.Count
        ' Copy the row to the clipboard
        ws.Rows(i).Copy
        
        ' Create a new page in Word and paste the row
        wrdDoc.Range.InsertBreak Type:=wdPageBreak
        wrdDoc.Range.Paste
        
        ' Move the insertion point to the beginning of the next page
        wrdApp.Selection.HomeKey wdStory
        
        ' Add a page break at the end of the last row
        If i = ws.UsedRange.Rows.Count Then
            wrdDoc.Range.InsertBreak Type:=wdPageBreak
        End If
    Next i
    
    ' Clean up the objects
    Set wrdDoc = Nothing
    wrdApp.Quit
    Set wrdApp = Nothing
End Sub
```
This macro assumes that your worksheet is named "Sheet1". If your worksheet has a different name, you'll need to change the line `Set ws = wb.Worksheets("Sheet1")` to match the name of your worksheet.

Also, note that this macro uses the default font and formatting in Word. If you want to apply specific formatting to the rows when they're pasted into Word, you'll need to modify the macro accordingly.

Distinguish between green house effect and global warming

The greenhouse effect and global warming are two related but distinct phenomena related to climate change.

The greenhouse effect is a naturally occurring process where greenhouse gases, such as carbon dioxide, methane, and water vapor, trap heat in the Earth's atmosphere and regulate the planet's temperature. This effect is essential for maintaining a stable climate and is responsible for the Earth's ability to support life.

However, human activities, such as the burning of fossil fuels and deforestation, have increased the concentration of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere, leading to an enhancement of the greenhouse effect. This enhancement is known as global warming.

Global warming refers to the long-term rise in the average surface temperature of the Earth due to human activities and the resulting increase in greenhouse gas emissions. This rise in temperature has significant impacts on the planet, including rising sea levels, more frequent and intense heat waves, changes in precipitation patterns, and the loss of biodiversity.

In conclusion, the greenhouse effect is a naturally occurring process that is vital for life on Earth, while global warming is the result of human activities that are enhancing the greenhouse effect and leading to negative impacts on the environment and society.

The object P represents the intersection of the two microservices A and B, and the morphisms p and q represent the projection of the data in P onto A and B, respectively.

We can use the pullback to reason about the behavior of the composed microservice C. For example, we can use the pullback to ensure that data is consistent between the two microservices A and B, and to ensure that any updates to the data in A or B are propagated correctly to C.

Similarly, we can use pushouts to model the composition of microservices that represent different parts of an ecommerce system. A pushout is a dual concept to the pullback, which represents the union of two categories.

In a pushout diagram, we have three categories: A, B, and C, and two functors f: A → C and g: B → C. The pushout is a universal construction that defines an object P and two morphisms p: A → P and q: B → P, such that f ∘ p = g ∘ q. The object P represents the union of the two microservices A and B, and the morphisms p and q represent the inclusion of the data in A and B, respectively.

Cloud vendors are likely to continue to transform the networking domain in the coming years, in several key ways:

1. Cloud-based networking solutions are becoming increasingly popular, as they enable companies to easily and securely connect their on-premises networks with the public cloud. This allows organizations to more easily migrate workloads and data to the cloud, and to take advantage of the scalability, reliability, and cost-efficiency of cloud-based services.
2. Network function virtualization (NFV) and software-defined networking (SDN) technologies are becoming more widely adopted, enabling organizations to more easily and flexibly manage and control their network infrastructure. This can improve network performance and reliability, and reduce the need for manual intervention by IT staff.
4. Network security is becoming increasingly important, as more and more data and applications are moved to the cloud. Cloud vendors are investing in advanced security technologies and practices, such as encryption, firewalls, and intrusion detection and prevention systems, to help protect their customers' networks and data from cyber threats.

Overall, the next 5+ years are likely to see continued innovation and transformation in the networking domain, as cloud vendors continue to develop and deploy new technologies and solutions to help organizations more easily and securely connect and manage their networks.
What is SDN?

Software-defined networking (SDN) is a networking architecture that separates the control plane (which makes decisions about how data should be routed) from the data plane (which actually forwards the data). This allows network administrators to more easily and flexibly manage and control their network infrastructure, by using a central, software-based controller to make decisions about how data should be routed across the network.

SDN allows network administrators to quickly and dynamically respond to changing network demands, and to better integrate their networks with other cloud-based services. It also enables the use of network function virtualization (NFV), which allows network functions (such as firewalls, load balancers, and intrusion detection systems) to be implemented in software, rather than in dedicated hardware. This can improve network performance and reliability, and reduce costs.

Overall, SDN is a key technology for enabling the agile, flexible, and scalable networking architectures that are required for modern, cloud-based environments.

```python
import numpy as np
```

```python
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
from glove import Corpus, Glove
def create_glove_embeddings_and_plot(df):
    # Create a corpus from the text data
    corpus = Corpus()
    for sentence in df['text']:
        corpus.fit(sentence.split(), window=5)

    # Train the GloVe word embedding model
    glove = Glove(no_components=300, learning_rate=0.05)
    glove.fit(corpus.matrix, epochs=30, no_threads=4, verbose=True)
    glove.add_dictionary(corpus.dictionary)

    # Get the word vectors and tokens
    tokens = glove.dictionary.keys()
    word_vectors = np.array([glove.word_vectors[glove.dictionary[token]] for token in tokens])

    # Perform PCA on the word vectors to reduce dimensionality to 2
    pca = PCA(n_components=2)
    word_vectors_pca = pca.fit_transform(word_vectors)

    # Plot the word vectors as a 2D scatter plot
    fig, ax = plt.subplots()
    ax.scatter(word_vectors_pca[:, 0], word_vectors_pca[:, 1])
    for i, token in enumerate(tokens):
        ax.annotate(token, xy=(word_vectors_pca[i, 0], word_vectors_pca[i, 1]))

    plt.show()
```

```python
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

def plot_spacy_embedding(model, words):
    """
    This function takes in a spacy word2vec model and a list of words and generates a 2D scatter plot of the word embeddings.

    Args:
    1. model: spacy.lang.en.English - The spacy word2vec model.
    2. words: list - The list of words to be plotted.

    Returns:
    None - Displays the scatter plot of the word embeddings.
    """
    
    # Get embeddings for words
    embeddings = np.array([model(word).vector for word in words])
    
    # Reduce dimensions to 2D
    pca = PCA(n_components=2)
    pca.fit(embeddings)
    pca_features = pca.transform(embeddings)

    # Plot the 2D embeddings
    plt.figure(figsize=(10, 10))
    plt.scatter(pca_features[:, 0], pca_features[:, 1], marker='o')

    # Add labels for the points
    for i, word in enumerate(words):
        plt.annotate(word, xy=(pca_features[i, 0], pca_features[i, 1]))
        
    plt.show()
```

Give 1 advantage of a ring main circuit

One advantage of a ring main circuit is that it allows for a more efficient distribution of electrical power, as it provides multiple paths for electricity to flow. This reduces the risk of voltage drops and ensures that power can be delivered more evenly throughout the circuit.
What is the function of a live wire

The function of a live wire in an electrical circuit is to provide a path for the flow of electrical current from the power source (such as a generator or battery) to the electrical device or appliance. The live wire is typically colored brown or red and is one of the two main wires in a power cable, with the other being the neutral wire. The live wire carries the alternating current (AC) with a voltage of around 230 volts in the UK, and it is the wire that poses a danger of electric shock if touched.
What is the function of a neutral wire

The function of a neutral wire in an electrical circuit is to provide a return path for electrical current after it has passed through an electrical device. It carries the current back to the power source or electrical supply, completing the circuit. The neutral wire is often connected to earth ground at the point of supply to provide additional safety. In contrast to the live wire, which carries the electrical current from the source, the neutral wire has a voltage close to 0 volts, and it is usually colored blue in the UK and other countries that use similar electrical wiring standards.
What is the function of a earth wire

The function of an earth wire is to provide a low resistance path for electric current to flow to the ground in the event of a fault in an electrical appliance or circuit. This is a safety measure that helps to prevent electric shocks and fires by ensuring that any stray electrical current is safely conducted away from the user or the electrical system. The earth wire is connected to the metal casing of an appliance and to a grounding rod or plate that is buried in the ground, and provides a direct path for current to flow back to the earth if a fault occurs.
What does MCB stand for and how does it work

MCB stands for Miniature Circuit Breaker.

An MCB is an automatically operated electrical switch designed to protect an electrical circuit from damage caused by excess current from an overload or short circuit. The MCB is connected in series with the circuit it is designed to protect, and when there is an overload or short circuit, the MCB trips and disconnects the circuit. This helps to prevent overheating and other damage that could occur if the circuit were allowed to continue to operate with too much current flowing through it. MCBs are commonly used in residential and commercial electrical installations to protect circuits and prevent electrical fires.

This can lead to a narrow and skewed understanding of the world, as the individual is not exposed to diverse perspectives or new information.

An echo chamber, on the other hand, refers to a situation where an individual or group is surrounded by sources of information that all reinforce the same views and opinions. In this case, the individual or group is not only seeking out information that confirms their existing beliefs, but they are also receiving it from multiple sources, leading to a reinforced and amplified effect.

To give an example, imagine a person who only watches news channels that share their political views, and actively avoids those that do not. This person is in an information cocoon, as they are only exposed to a narrow range of perspectives. Now imagine a group of people who all share the same political views, and only communicate with each other through social media platforms that reinforce their views.         # Add a flow entry to allow traffic from the subscriber to go into the ONU
```python
        olt.cmd("ovs-ofctl add-flow olt in_port=1,dl_type=0x0800,nw_src=10.0.0.3,nw_dst=10.0.0.2,actions=output:2")

if __name__ == '__main__':

    net = Mininet(topo=topo, controller=RemoteController, link=TCLink, switch=OVSSwitch)
```

Summary : Posthumanism and transhumanism are philosophies that envision possible relations between humans and posthumans. Critical versions of posthumanism and transhumanism examine the idea of potential threats involved in human–posthuman interactions (i.e., species extinction, species domination, AI takeover) and propose precautionary measures against these threats by elaborating protocols for the prosocial use of technology. Critics of these philosophies usually argue against the reality of the threats or dispute the feasibility of the proposed measures. We take this debate back to its modern roots. The play that gave the world the term “robot” (R.U.R.: Rossum’s Universal Robots) is nowadays remembered mostly as a particular instance of an absurd apocalyptic vision about the doom of the human species through technology. However, we demonstrate that Karel Capek assumed that a negative interpretation of human–posthuman interactions emerges mainly from the human inability to think clearly about extinction, spirituality, and technology. We propose that the conflictual interpretation of human–posthuman interactions can be overcome by embracing Capek’s religiously and philosophically-inspired theory of altruism remediated by technology. We argue that this reinterpretation of altruism may strengthen the case for a more positive outlook on human–posthuman interactions.

What is normalization? Define first, second and third normal forms.

Normalization is the process of organizing a database in a way that reduces redundancy and dependency. It is a technique used to design and structure a database in a way that eliminates data redundancy, improves data integrity, and makes it easier to maintain and update.

There are several different levels of normalization, known as normal forms. The three most commonly used normal forms are:

1. First normal form (1NF): A database is in 1NF if it satisfies the following conditions:
	* All data is stored in a table, with each row representing a unique entity.
	* Each column represents a single attribute.
	* There are no repeating groups of data within a table.
2. Second normal form (2NF): A database is in 2NF if it satisfies the following conditions:
	* It is already in 1NF.
	* All non-key attributes are fully dependent on the primary key.
3. Third normal form (3NF): A database is in 3NF if it satisfies the following conditions:
	* It is already in 2NF.
	* There are no transitive dependencies between non-key attributes.

Normalization is an important technique for designing and organizing a database, as it helps to eliminate data redundancy, improve data integrity, and make it easier to maintain and update the database.
